Cutting across the Cloth

A costume workshop examined a piece of ____1____ fabric made by interlacing two sets of threads. The threads running along the length were called the ____2____. The threads crossing them from side to side were the ____3____. These names concerned the fabric's structure, not the eventual shape of a sleeve.

The finished edge that resisted unravelling was the ____4____. It gave beginners a useful reference for the lengthwise direction. The tutor asked them to draw a line ____5____ to that edge, keeping the same direction without crossing it. A line at a right angle would instead be perpendicular.

The direction of the threads was the fabric's ____6____. A pattern piece could be positioned in relation to it before cutting. The tutor then drew a ____7____ line across the sample, running obliquely rather than following either thread system. Cutting on the true ____8____ meant using the direction halfway between the lengthwise and crosswise threads.

For this sample, the diagonal direction allowed more ____9____ under the same gentle pull. That behaviour could help a garment follow a curved shape, but it could also affect how the piece hung. The class did not assume that every fabric would behave identically.

After cutting, a raw edge could ____10____, with loose threads separating from it. Pupils therefore practised finishing edges as well as choosing a cutting direction. A neat outline on paper did not by itself establish how the actual cloth would move or survive handling. The exercise connected the pattern to the material rather than treating fabric as a completely uniform sheet.

The Dots under the Frond

A botanical garden displayed a fern with brown dots beneath its leaves. A visitor assumed that the plant was ill. The gardener explained that the broad leaves were called ____1____ and that the dots in this example were normal reproductive structures rather than signs of infection.

The dots were arranged in ____2____, groups of smaller structures. Within tiny ____3____, the plant produced reproductive cells called ____4____. Unlike the seeds of a flowering plant, these cells did not contain the same kind of developed embryo and stored food arrangement. The explanation concerned this fern's life cycle rather than calling every brown mark on any plant harmless.

When conditions were suitable, the released cells could ____5____ and begin a new stage of growth. They generally needed a sufficiently ____6____ environment, with water available, rather than a permanently dry surface. A later stage would eventually lead to another recognisable fern.

The plant's underground horizontal stem was a ____7____. Its ____8____ took up water and helped anchor it. A stem growing below the soil and the organs absorbing water were not the same structure, even though both could be hidden from view.

The movement of reproductive cells away from the parent was ____9____. This could help them reach other locations, but arriving somewhere did not guarantee successful growth. The garden labelled the illustrated plant as ____10____ because it had reached the stage of producing reproductive structures.

The visitor left with a different question. Instead of treating every unfamiliar feature as damage, she could ask what role it played in the plant's development. The gardener also stressed limits: a general account of reproduction did not replace examining a plant that showed other evidence of disease.

A Coating Changed by Heat

A ceramics class compared an unfinished cup with a fired sample. The coating intended to form a glassy surface was the ____1____. Before application, finely divided materials were mixed with water to make a ____2____, a suspension that could be brushed onto the clay body.

The class used a ____3____, a chamber designed for controlled heating, rather than an ordinary drying cupboard. The high-temperature treatment was called ____4____. Simply leaving the wet coating to dry in room air did not reproduce that process.

The tutor recorded ____5____ throughout the cycle to describe how hot the chamber became. Under the specified conditions, some coating materials could ____6____, becoming liquid enough to flow together. The resulting surface depended on composition as well as the heating history, so a single maximum reading did not fully describe every outcome.

The sample's bare foot remained ____7____, without the glassy coating, so it could rest on an appropriate support during the prepared demonstration. The uncoated body was more ____8____, containing accessible pores through which liquid could enter, than the particular glazed surface being compared.

During ____9____, the temperature fell after heating. The body and coating did not necessarily contract by identical amounts. A mismatch could contribute to ____10____, visible breaks in the finished surface. Those marks needed examination rather than being automatically praised as decoration.

The lesson did not claim that every glazed vessel was suitable for holding food or that every visible crack had the same cause. It connected material, treatment and observed result within the examples supplied. Students learned to describe the coating and the underlying body separately before judging the whole cup by its colour or shine.

Returning to the Mark

A beginner ensemble rehearsed from a written score. The system of signs representing musical instructions was ____1____. Five horizontal lines formed a ____2____ on which notes could be placed. Their vertical position helped indicate ____3____, how high or low a sound was, under the stated clef.

A vertical ____4____ separated one segment from the next. In this score, each segment was a ____5____ containing the required count of beats. The class avoided assuming that every segment in every piece had the same pattern.

A double mark with dots instructed players to ____6____ a section, going back and performing it again. It did not mean that the music should become faster. Speed was associated with ____7____, while patterns of long and short events concerned rhythm.

The score also included ____8____, signs specifying moments without a played note. These were counted in time rather than treated as a chance to stop following the piece. The written ____9____ of a rest indicated how long that interval lasted.

Instructions about loudness belonged to ____10____. A gradual increase could be marked with a growing wedge. The tutor kept loudness separate from speed: playing more strongly did not automatically require accelerating.

At the end of rehearsal, the group followed the repeat correctly without losing its place during rests. The improvement came from connecting several kinds of instruction rather than memorising the shapes of isolated signs. The score guided an interpretation, but it did not contain every detail of sound and ensemble coordination by itself.

An Outcome Not Yet Observed

A methods course examined time until a specified outcome after treatment. The occurrence defined for analysis was the ____1____. For each participant, the recorded ____2____ measured elapsed time from the chosen starting point. That origin had to be stated; dates collected for administrative convenience were not automatically comparable follow-up times.

Some participants remained free of the outcome when observation ended. Their records were subject to right ____3____: the event time was not known exactly, but it exceeded the observed follow-up. The course distinguished this from treating those participants as if the event had occurred at their last visit.

The ____4____ function described the probability of remaining event-free beyond a specified time. By contrast, the ____5____ was an instantaneous event rate conditional on having remained event-free up to that point. It was not simply the probability of the event over the entire study.

A measured characteristic used to explain variation was a ____6____. The model could relate such characteristics to the outcome process under its stated assumptions. The ____7____ pattern provided a reference for specified covariate values; it did not mean that every participant had identical underlying risk.

Inference depended on how observation ended. A claim of ____8____ censoring required a defensible relation between the censoring and event processes, possibly conditional on measured features. An unreturned questionnaire did not establish that relation by itself.

The investigators used the observed information to ____9____ quantities of interest. When estimable, the ____10____ survival time marked the point associated with half the relevant distribution, not the arithmetic average of all observed follow-up lengths.

The seminar emphasised that choosing a standard method did not remove the need to examine the observation process. The endpoint, time origin and assumptions about incomplete follow-up determined what a resulting curve could support. People still under observation without the event contributed information, even though their final event times were not available.

The Machine Was Still Working

An accounting seminar considered a machine bought for use over several years. The organisation recognised it as an ____1____, a resource expected to provide future economic benefits under the example's framework. Recording it in that category did not imply that its value would remain unchanged.

The payment reduced ____2____ when the purchase was settled. The annual allocation of the machine's depreciable amount, however, was ____3____. That accounting allocation was not another payment to the supplier each year. The students separated the timing of money movement from the periods receiving the reported cost.

The estimated ____4____ life described how long the machine was expected to serve the organisation. Its ____5____ value was the estimated amount recoverable at the end of that use after relevant disposal costs, under the assumptions supplied. Neither estimate had to equal the period for which the machine could physically exist.

Under the specified ____6____-line method, equal amounts were allocated across the stated periods. The resulting annual ____7____ entered the accounts for that period, even when no corresponding cash payment occurred then. The method was an allocation convention rather than a measurement of the machine's resale price every morning.

The total allocation recognised so far was ____8____ depreciation. Subtracting it, together with relevant adjustments, contributed to the machine's ____9____ amount in the accounts. That figure was not automatically an offer obtainable from a buyer.

An unexpected loss in recoverable value could require an ____10____ assessment under the framework. Such a review addressed a different issue from the routine scheduled allocation. The example therefore distinguished continued physical operation, accounting allocation and recoverability. A machine could still work while an accounting estimate changed, and an unchanged estimate did not demonstrate that no wear or market change had occurred.

An accounting seminar considered a machine bought for use over several years. The organisation recognised it as an ____1____, a resource expected to provide future economic benefits under the example's framework. Recording it in that category did not imply that its value would remain unchanged.

The payment reduced ____2____ when the purchase was settled. The annual allocation of the machine's depreciable amount, however, was ____3____. That accounting allocation was not another payment to the supplier each year. The students separated the timing of money movement from the periods receiving the reported cost.

The estimated ____4____ life described how long the machine was expected to serve the organisation. Its ____5____ value was the estimated amount recoverable at the end of that use after relevant disposal costs, under the assumptions supplied. Neither estimate had to equal the period for which the machine could physically exist.

Under the specified ____6____-line method, equal amounts were allocated across the stated periods. The resulting annual ____7____ entered the accounts for that period, even when no corresponding cash payment occurred then. The method was an allocation convention rather than a measurement of the machine's resale price every morning.

The total allocation recognised so far was ____8____ depreciation. Subtracting it, together with relevant adjustments, contributed to the machine's ____9____ amount in the accounts. That figure was not automatically an offer obtainable from a buyer.

An unexpected loss in recoverable value could require an ____10____ assessment under the framework. Such a review addressed a different issue from the routine scheduled allocation. The example therefore distinguished continued physical operation, accounting allocation and recoverability. A machine could still work while an accounting estimate changed, and an unchanged estimate did not demonstrate that no wear or market change had occurred.

Allowed into the Record

A legal reasoning class used a fictional hearing with expressly stated rules. Material was ____1____ if those rules permitted the decision-maker to consider it. Permission to consider an item did not establish that the item was correct or that it settled the case.

The first question concerned ____2____: whether the item bore on a fact that mattered to the dispute. Another question concerned ____3____, whether a document was what its presenter claimed it to be. A genuine document could still contain an inaccurate statement, so these inquiries were kept distinct.

A witness's spoken account was ____4____. The class evaluated the witness's ____5____, including reasons to trust or doubt the account in the circumstances. Confidence of delivery was treated as one observation, not a guarantee of accuracy.

The opposing representative could use ____6____-examination to test the account through questions. An additional independent source supporting a material point could provide ____7____. Repeating the same rumour through several speakers was not automatically independent support.

The rules assigned a ____8____ of proof to a particular party. They also specified the ____9____ of proof, the degree of persuasion required for the relevant finding. Who had to establish a point and how strongly it had to be established were different dimensions.

Finally, the decision-maker assessed the ____10____ to give each admitted item. This was its persuasive significance in the whole case, not simply whether it had entered the record. The exercise avoided claiming that these fictional procedures described every jurisdiction. Its purpose was to separate several judgements often compressed into the phrase good evidence. Admission, identity, reliability and persuasion could interact without being interchangeable.

More Than a Polite Ending

A sociolinguistics seminar examined a language with contrasting ways of addressing the same person. In the constructed examples, a speaker could use a respectful form to show ____1____ towards an addressee. The form was not merely a longer way to express the sentence's factual ____2____, the claim about what had happened.

The choice belonged to a social ____3____, a pattern of language associated with a situation and relationship. It could ____4____ rank or formality, signalling a social relation without stating it as a separate descriptive sentence. The seminar distinguished this verb from the idea that every form mechanically revealed a speaker's inner attitude.

An institution's ____5____ organised relative positions such as supervisor and junior member. Yet rank alone did not determine every choice. Speakers could use a familiar form to express ____6____, shared affiliation and closeness, even when their official positions differed.

In another exchange, a normally respectful form created unexpected ____7____ between old friends. That effect depended on their usual practice and the immediate ____8____, including the surrounding conversation. Reading the form in isolation would miss why it seemed marked.

The class also considered ____9____ use, in which an exaggerated respectful expression conveyed an evaluation different from straightforward respect. Listeners relied on tone and circumstances rather than reversing every respectful form automatically.

A term of ____10____ such as a title or personal name offered another resource for managing the relationship. The analysis kept grammatical form, social expectation and local interpretation in view together. It did not rank the language as inherently more polite than languages using different resources. Courtesy and conflict could both be communicated through forms that a simple translation table might label respectful.

A sociolinguistics seminar examined a language with contrasting ways of addressing the same person. In the constructed examples, a speaker could use a respectful form to show ____1____ towards an addressee. The form was not merely a longer way to express the sentence's factual ____2____, the claim about what had happened.

The choice belonged to a social ____3____, a pattern of language associated with a situation and relationship. It could ____4____ rank or formality, signalling a social relation without stating it as a separate descriptive sentence. The seminar distinguished this verb from the idea that every form mechanically revealed a speaker's inner attitude.

An institution's ____5____ organised relative positions such as supervisor and junior member. Yet rank alone did not determine every choice. Speakers could use a familiar form to express ____6____, shared affiliation and closeness, even when their official positions differed.

In another exchange, a normally respectful form created unexpected ____7____ between old friends. That effect depended on their usual practice and the immediate ____8____, including the surrounding conversation. Reading the form in isolation would miss why it seemed marked.

The class also considered ____9____ use, in which an exaggerated respectful expression conveyed an evaluation different from straightforward respect. Listeners relied on tone and circumstances rather than reversing every respectful form automatically.

A term of ____10____ such as a title or personal name offered another resource for managing the relationship. The analysis kept grammatical form, social expectation and local interpretation in view together. It did not rank the language as inherently more polite than languages using different resources. Courtesy and conflict could both be communicated through forms that a simple translation table might label respectful.
